hero.title: An AI-native video editing workspace.
hero.p1: Vibed is a video editor you talk to. Describe the edit you want and it happens — no menu hunting, no dragging handles across a timeline.
hero.p2: Everything a creator needs to take raw footage to a finished cut lives in one place, and the AI understands all of it.

problem.p1: Video editing is fragmented. A single video pulls a creator across four different kinds of work, each in its own tool, none of which know about the others.

items.title: Editing
items.body: Cutting, trimming, framing — mechanical work that eats the majority of the time and contributes the least to the result.

items.title: Scripting
items.body: Transcripts, captions, structure. Usually a separate document, disconnected from the footage it describes.

items.title: Organisation
items.body: Naming, sorting and finding clips across shoots. The tax you pay before real work starts.

items.title: Storytelling
items.body: The part that actually matters — and the first thing to get squeezed when the other three run long.

problem.p2: The tools are powerful. The gaps between them are where the time goes.

solution.p1: Vibed closes those gaps by putting four systems in one workspace and letting them share context.

items.title: Timeline
items.body: A real editor — multi-track, non-destructive, with full undo. Nothing the AI does is permanent, and nothing happens you can't reverse.

items.title: AI Assistant
items.body: Plain-language commands. "Remove the silences." "Cut between speakers." It plans the edit, shows you the plan, and waits for your approval before touching anything.

items.title: Brain
items.body: Reads the state of your project and suggests what to do next — based on what you've already done, not a fixed checklist.

items.title: Media Intelligence
items.body: Analyses footage on upload: who's speaking, what's in frame, where the usable takes are. That understanding is what makes the other three specific rather than generic.

solution.p2: Because they share one context, an instruction like "tighten this up" means something concrete instead of something vague.

vision.p1: The interface most editors inherited was designed for cutting physical film. It's precise, and it's slow, and it makes you translate creative intent into hundreds of small mechanical operations.
vision.p2: We think that translation step is the problem, not the craft. The goal isn't to remove the editor — it's to remove everything between having an idea and seeing it on screen.

items.title: You stay in control
items.body: The AI suggests and executes. You decide. Every action is visible, named, and reversible. Nothing happens inside a black box.

items.title: Work in your tools
items.body: You don't have to abandon Premiere, Final Cut, or DaVinci. Vibed works with the suite you already finish in — not instead of it.

items.title: Editing is creative work
items.body: The mechanical parts — silence removal, cleanup, formatting — shouldn't take your attention. The story should.

items.title: Your footage is yours
items.body: We store it, we process it, we delete it on your schedule. We never train on it and we never sell it.

audience.p1: Podcasters, YouTubers, interviewers and documentary makers — anyone working with long-form talking footage where the edit is mostly about finding the good parts and cutting the rest.
audience.p2: If you spend more time on cleanup than on story, Vibed is built for you.

founder.name: Marc Guidjol
founder.bio: Vibed started with a creator who got tired of editing the hard way. The idea took shape in Istanbul in 2024, and the engineering came together at Epitech in Paris — first as a footage analysis tool, then, once the real gap became obvious, as a conversational editing environment.
